name: The Transfiguration of Christ
description: Jesus is transfigured on the mountain and his divinity is revealed.
biblicalBasis: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured: his face shines like the sun, and his clothes become white as light (Matt 17:1-9, Mark 9:2-10, Luke 9:28-36). Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him about his "departure" in Jerusalem. Peter wants to build three shelters. A bright cloud overshadows them, and a voice says: "This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!" On the way down, Jesus forbids them to tell anyone about the vision until the Son of Man has risen.
significance: The Transfiguration reveals who Jesus truly is — God's glory breaks through his human form. Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) testify about him and speak of his "departure" (exodus) in Jerusalem — his death on the cross as a new exodus from slavery. The event is a foretaste of the glory of the resurrection, given to the disciples as strength before the path of suffering.
liturgicalContext: White color. Placed right before Lent — a glimpse of glory before the journey of suffering begins. The last Sunday of Epiphanytide. The contrast is intentional: from the light of the mountain to the temptation in the wilderness (1st Sunday in Lent).
history: The Transfiguration has been celebrated in the Eastern Church since the 5th century (August 6). In the Western Church, it was officially instituted in 1457 by Pope Callixtus III. The Lutheran tradition places it as the conclusion of Epiphanytide, as a final turning point before Lent.
otConnections: Moses on Sinai where his face shone after meeting God (Exod 34:29-35). Elijah on Horeb where God revealed himself (1 Kings 19). The cloud as a sign of God's presence — the tabernacle cloud (Exod 40:34-38) and the temple cloud (1 Kings 8:10-11). Daniel's vision of the Son of Man in glory (Dan 7:13-14).

references.reason: Matt 16:24-28 is the direct introduction to the Transfiguration of Christ (Matt 17). Jesus warns that some will see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom before they die, and calls the disciples to take up their cross. This is the main text for the Feast of the Transfiguration in many liturgical traditions, as it sets the stage for the divine revelation that occurs six days later.

This is the central account of the Transfiguration of Christ (the Transfiguration). The text describes Jesus being transformed, the meeting with Moses and Elijah, and the voice from the cloud confirming Jesus' divinity. This is the main text for this feast day.

Here Jesus explains the connection between Elijah and John the Baptist, which is an important theological part of the Transfiguration event and the preparation for suffering. This links directly to the prophecy that Elijah must come before the Messiah.

The healing of the boy with a demon illustrates the contrast between the disciples' weak faith (which could not cast out the demon) and the divine glory they saw on the mountain. It emphasizes the need for prayer and fasting (v. 21) and the faith necessary to face the suffering predicted in vv. 22-23.

Immediately after the Transfiguration, Jesus gives a new prediction of his suffering. This underscores the contrast between the glory of the mountain and the way to the cross, which is a central theme in the meaning of the Transfiguration (preparation for suffering).

The incident with the temple tax is the concluding part of the chapter and shows Jesus as Lord over the temple and its tax. It links back to the temple and Moses/Elijah on the mountain, completing the theological unity of Matthew 17.
